description: HN.NASA is a team of three members: Nguyen Bui Gia Huy, Dao Nam Anh, and Do Minh Quang. We share a passion for programming, technology, and innovation. With creativity, teamwork, and a strong desire to learn, we enjoy exploring new ideas, solving challenges, and turning our ideas into reality through technology. Our goal is to develop useful and innovative products together.
summary:
NASA Technical Academy, developed by team HN.NASA (NS13001) from FPT High School Tây Hà Nội, is an interactive STEM educational game that introduces students to real space technologies through engineering simulations.

Players take on the role of space technicians, completing missions involving five technologies: the Perseverance Mars Rover, Landsat 9 satellite, International Space Station, Canadarm2 robotic arm, and Hubble Space Telescope. They diagnose technical faults, assemble and repair components, operate equipment, analyze scientific data, and manage limited budgets. Each device features different gameplay activities based on its real-world functions. Players must balance cost, performance, reliability, compatibility, and safety to complete missions successfully.

The project addresses the challenge of making complex STEM concepts more engaging and practical. Instead of relying on memorization and multiple-choice questions, it allows students to learn through hands-on experimentation, decision-making, and problem-solving.

NASA Technical Academy is important because it connects classroom knowledge with real engineering applications, develops critical thinking and technical skills, and inspires students to explore space science, robotics, and engineering careers.
details:
Project Details

1. Team Information

  • Team Name: HN.NASA
  • Team Code: NS13001
  • School: FPT High School Tây Hà Nội (THPT FPT Tây Hà Nội)
  • Project Name: NASA Technical Academy
  • Project Category: Educational Technology / STEM / Space Exploration

2. Project Overview

NASA Technical Academy is an interactive educational simulation game designed to introduce students to space technology, engineering, and scientific problem-solving.

In this game, players take on the role of space engineers and technical specialists. Their responsibility is to inspect equipment, identify technical problems, assemble components, perform repairs, operate systems, and complete missions involving real space technologies.

Instead of simply reading information or answering multiple-choice questions, players learn by interacting directly with simulated equipment. They must understand how different components work, investigate technical symptoms, make engineering decisions, and observe the consequences of their actions.

The game is built around five real NASA-related space technologies:

  1. Perseverance Mars Rover: A robotic vehicle designed to explore the surface of Mars, collect samples, and conduct scientific research.
  2. Landsat 9 Earth Observation Satellite: A satellite that collects images and scientific data about Earth's surface and environmental changes.
  3. International Space Station (ISS): An orbital research laboratory that supports scientific experiments and human spaceflight.
  4. Canadarm2: A robotic arm used aboard the International Space Station to move cargo, support astronauts, and assist with maintenance.
  5. Hubble Space Telescope: A space telescope used to observe distant objects and investigate the universe.

Each device has its own missions, technical systems, and gameplay activities. Players select a mission and enter the gameplay directly, without introductory videos before missions.

3. How the Game Works

The game follows an interactive engineering simulation approach. Players are given a technical situation, equipment condition, available resources, and mission objectives. They must determine what is wrong and decide how to solve the problem.

Depending on the device and mission, players may need to:

  • Assemble and repair equipment: Select, drag, place, rotate, and connect components in the correct positions.
  • Connect electrical circuits: Link wires to appropriate ports, restore electrical connections, and test whether a system works.
  • Operate technical controls: Use switches, buttons, sliders, levers, and virtual joysticks to control equipment.
  • Analyze scientific data: Examine satellite images, thermal maps, signals, charts, and other technical information to identify problems.
  • Arrange procedures: Organize technical steps in the correct sequence to complete maintenance or operating tasks.
  • Manage resources: Allocate limited energy, materials, time, and money to keep systems functioning.
  • Perform precision operations: Control robotic equipment and other mechanisms that require accurate movement and positioning.

The game is not limited to selecting answers from a list. Players must perform actions and interact with the simulated systems. Their decisions affect the equipment's condition and the progress of the mission.

4. Different Gameplay for Each Space Technology

A key design principle is that each device must have gameplay based on its real-world purpose. The five missions are not simply the same robot-control activity with different graphics.

Perseverance Mars Rover

Players work with the Mars rover's mobility, cameras, robotic arm, scientific instruments, sample collection system, and communication systems.

Possible activities include:

  • Operating the rover to navigate simulated Martian terrain.
  • Inspecting camera images and identifying obstacles.
  • Using the robotic arm to interact with scientific targets.
  • Collecting and handling samples.
  • Diagnosing communication problems and restoring data transmission.

Landsat 9 Earth Observation Satellite

Players work with Earth observation systems rather than controlling a ground vehicle.

Possible activities include:

  • Analyzing satellite images to identify environmental changes.
  • Examining thermal information collected by the Thermal Infrared Sensor (TIRS-2).
  • Inspecting the Operational Land Imager (OLI-2) and thermal imaging systems.
  • Identifying sensor faults and restoring observation capabilities.
  • Managing observation schedules and data transmission.

International Space Station (ISS)

Players maintain essential station systems and manage the resources required to support operations in orbit.

Possible activities include:

  • Managing electrical power distribution.
  • Monitoring thermal regulation systems.
  • Maintaining communication equipment.
  • Allocating limited resources.
  • Diagnosing faults that affect station operations and life-support-related systems.

Canadarm2

Players operate a robotic arm through its joints and control systems.

Possible activities include:

  • Controlling individual robotic arm joints.
  • Grappling and moving simulated cargo.
  • Calibrating joints and correcting positioning errors.
  • Using cameras to inspect the working area.
  • Diagnosing mechanical faults that affect movement and precision.

Hubble Space Telescope

Players work with astronomical observation and telescope systems.

Possible activities include:

  • Analyzing astronomical images.
  • Adjusting simulated focus and observation settings.
  • Calibrating pointing and stability systems.
  • Managing observation schedules and available energy.
  • Diagnosing problems that affect image quality and observation accuracy.

5. Realistic Engineering Challenges and Component System

One of the main features of NASA Technical Academy is its component selection and engineering decision system.

Components are not differentiated by price alone. Different options have different characteristics, including:

  • Purchase cost.
  • Durability.
  • Reliability.
  • Performance.
  • Compatibility.
  • Maintenance requirements.
  • Long-term operating costs.

Players can choose between budget, standard, and premium components. Each option involves advantages and disadvantages.

For example, a cheaper component may reduce initial expenses but have lower reliability or require more maintenance. A premium component may perform better but consume a larger part of the available budget.

Compatibility is also important. Installing an incompatible component can prevent a system from functioning correctly.

The game includes technical dependencies between components. When a component is damaged, the functions that depend on it are affected, while unrelated systems should remain operational.

Examples:

  • A damaged camera prevents the corresponding camera view from working.
  • A damaged wheel motor affects the rover's movement.
  • A communication system failure prevents data transmission.
  • A faulty Canadarm2 joint affects the corresponding robotic movement.
  • An electrical power problem limits the operation of dependent ISS systems.
  • A pointing or stability problem affects Hubble's observation accuracy.

Before certain operations, players must check whether their equipment is ready. Unsafe or incompatible configurations can trigger warnings or prevent an operation from proceeding.

These mechanics encourage players to understand the relationships between components instead of simply replacing everything with the most expensive option.

6. Budget and Resource Management

Players must complete missions while working with limited budgets and resources.

They need to consider:

  • Initial component costs.
  • Repair and replacement expenses.
  • Maintenance costs.
  • Operating expenses.
  • Potential costs caused by equipment failure.
  • The balance between performance, reliability, and safety.

During the initial assembly stage, exceeding the available budget produces a warning rather than an immediate loss. Players can revise their selections, remove or replace components, and recalculate the total cost.

The initial assembly can only be confirmed when the total cost is within the budget. Spending exactly the available budget is allowed.

Other mission stages retain their own budget and resource-management rules.

This system teaches students that engineering is not simply about choosing the most powerful equipment. Engineers must make practical decisions while considering cost, quality, efficiency, compatibility, and safety.

7. Difficulty Progression and Scoring

The game is designed to become more challenging as players develop their technical understanding.

The difficulty progression includes:

  • Introductory level: A relatively simple fault with clear symptoms and a generous budget.
  • Technician level: More complicated symptoms and limited resources.
  • Engineer level: Multiple related problems, different repair options, and engineering trade-offs.
  • Expert level: Several simultaneous failures, tighter budgets, and decisions involving long-term system reliability.

Difficulty comes from technical reasoning, data analysis, resource management, and choosing appropriate solutions rather than hiding information or using unnecessarily complicated wording.

Player performance can be evaluated through:

  • Accuracy of fault diagnosis.
  • Quality and compatibility of selected components.
  • Total cost and resource efficiency.
  • Equipment performance.
  • Operational safety.
  • Mission completion.
  • Avoidance of preventable failures.

Choosing the most expensive components does not automatically guarantee the highest score.

At the end of a mission, players receive a report showing their results, expenses, equipment performance, safety considerations, successful decisions, and areas for improvement.

8. Educational Benefits and Intended Impact

NASA Technical Academy aims to make STEM education more interactive, practical, and engaging.

The project helps students develop:

  • Critical thinking: Investigating technical symptoms and identifying possible causes.
  • Problem-solving: Testing solutions and correcting mistakes.
  • Engineering knowledge: Understanding components, mechanisms, and system dependencies.
  • Scientific literacy: Working with images, measurements, signals, and technical information.
  • Decision-making: Comparing different solutions and evaluating their consequences.
  • Resource management: Working within financial and operational constraints.
  • Creativity: Exploring different approaches to solve engineering challenges.

The intended impact is to help students understand how science, mathematics, and engineering are applied to real-world space exploration.

By allowing students to experiment with simulated equipment, the game turns abstract technical concepts into practical learning experiences. It also aims to inspire curiosity about astronomy, robotics, aerospace engineering, and future STEM careers.

9. Technology and Development Tools

The project is developed using Google AI Studio as its development environment.

NASA-related websites, scientific publications, and educational resources are used as references for the five space technologies, their components, and their operating principles.

The project also uses real NASA-related photographs, scientific imagery, and technical diagrams where suitable and verifiable.

The confirmed development environment is Google AI Studio. The exact programming languages, frameworks, external libraries, and hardware used in the implementation should be specified according to the project's actual technical setup rather than assumed.

10. Interface and User Experience

The game is designed for students and uses a modern space-technology aesthetic.

Its interface aims to be:

  • Clear and easy to navigate.
  • Visually connected to real space missions and engineering environments.
  • Suitable for educational use.
  • Accessible to both Vietnamese and English-speaking players.

The game supports Vietnamese and English language options. Mission instructions, interface text, system messages, and other learning content should follow the selected language consistently.

The visual design uses a technology-inspired palette, including blue, navy, white, and selected cyan or orange accents. The Roboto font is used for readability.

The interface avoids overly childish cartoon styles and instead emphasizes realistic space equipment, technical illustrations, scientific data, and control-center-inspired visuals.

11. Creativity and Innovation

The main creative idea behind NASA Technical Academy is combining real space technologies with interactive engineering simulation.

Many educational games focus on presenting facts or testing memorized knowledge. This project takes a different approach: students must use information to operate systems, diagnose faults, select components, manage budgets, and complete practical challenges.

The project also introduces engineering trade-offs into educational gameplay. A technically correct solution is not necessarily the cheapest, and the cheapest solution is not always the safest or most reliable.

Each of the five technologies has its own gameplay mechanics, allowing students to explore different areas of engineering, including robotics, remote sensing, electrical systems, mechanical control, and astronomy.

By combining scientific accuracy, interactive activities, realistic constraints, and immediate feedback, NASA Technical Academy aims to create a more meaningful connection between classroom learning and real engineering applications.

12. Factors Considered During Development

The team considered several important factors:

  1. Scientific accuracy: Equipment, components, and technical information should reflect real space technologies.
  2. Educational value: Activities should help students understand and apply STEM concepts.
  3. Gameplay variety: Each device should have distinct interactions and mission objectives.
  4. Realistic consequences: Equipment faults and player decisions should affect the appropriate systems.
  5. Engineering trade-offs: Cost, reliability, compatibility, performance, and safety should all matter.
  6. Difficulty balance: Challenges should progress through increasingly complex reasoning and resource management.
  7. Accessibility: Instructions and interface elements should be understandable and readable.
  8. User experience: Controls should be functional, responsive, and easy to understand.
  9. Bilingual support: Vietnamese and English should be available throughout the game.
  10. Reliable visual references: Images and diagrams should represent the correct equipment and be properly attributed.

Conclusion

NASA Technical Academy is an educational STEM simulation that transforms space technology into an interactive engineering experience. Through five different space technologies, practical repair and operation activities, realistic component systems, and resource-management challenges, the project encourages students to think like engineers rather than simply memorize scientific facts.

The ultimate goal of HN.NASA is to make learning about space exploration more engaging while helping students develop the technical understanding, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills needed to explore the world of science and engineering.
